19.text: It seems to me that Mr. Jochelson has in mind the same high degree

20.text: of susceptibility when he calls attention to the fact that the young men of

21.text: the Yukaghir were said in ancient times to be exceedingly bashful, so much

22.text: so that they would die when a sudden affront was given them, even by their

23.text: own relatives.² The shamans possess this nervous sensitiveness in a still

24.text: higher degree than other people. This finds expression in the proverb that

25.text: shamans are even more “soft to die” than ordinary people.

26.text: While speaking of this subject, let me add, that the slightest lack of

27.text: harmony between the acts of the shamans and the mysterious call of their

28.text: “spirits” brings their life to an end. This is expressed by the Chukchee

29.text: when they say that “spirits” are very bad-tempered, and punish with imme-

30.text: diate death the slightest disobedience of the shaman, and that this is partic-

31.text: ularly so when the shaman is slow to carry out those orders which are in-

33.text: On the other hand, apart from the displeasure of his keˊlet, a shaman

34.text: is said to be “resistant to death” and especially “difficult to kill,” even when

35.text: vanquished by enemies. Thus, in a description of a murder which took place

36.text: in the Anui country in the nineties of the last century, the native, whose

37.text: words were written down verbatim, says, —

38.text: “With an incantation of theirs they made him sleep. While he was sleeping, they attacked

39.text: him from both sides. One cut his throat; the other stabbed him in the direction of the heart,

40.text: the source of life and death. Nevertheless he jumped up. But he had no arms. They were also

41.text: ‘knowing people;’ and thus they induced him, likewise by incantations, to leave the camp unarmed.
